procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 30.06.2023 of the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam in CRLA No.906 of 2023, affirming the order passed by the Special Judge and refusing to grant anticipatory bail to the appellant.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant challenged the order passed by the Special Judge before the High Court of Kerala. The High Court affirmed the Special Judge's order and refused to grant anticipatory bail to the appellant.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the Kerala High Court affirmed the Special Judge's decision to deny anticipatory bail. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court's order.

directions: For all the foregoing reasons, this appeal succeeds and is hereby allowed.
The impugned order passed by the High Court is hereby set aside.
The impugned order of the Special Court is upheld.

issue.issue_text: Whether courts should have the discretion to look into the materials upon which a complaint has been registered, in addition to the complaint itself, to determine if the ingredients of the offence are made out, thereby making the bar of Section 18 inapplicable.

facts: The case involved a complaint (FIR) that was based on publicly available digital materials, specifically a YouTube video and other content uploaded by the appellant.
Unlike cases that rely on witness testimony about an event, the entire incriminatory material that formed the basis of the complaint was readily available for the court's review.
law: Section 18 of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, creates a bar on granting anticipatory bail for offences under the Act.
This bar is not absolute. It only applies if the complaint or FIR makes out a 'prima facie case' for an offence under the Act.
The phrase in Section 18, "having committed an offence under this Act," means that the accusation must clearly disclose all the necessary ingredients of the offence for the bar to be triggered.
Courts have a duty to conduct a preliminary inquiry to verify if the averments in a complaint prima facie constitute an offence under the Act.
application: The Court reasoned that to determine if a 'prima facie case' exists, it should not be limited to just the text of the complaint, especially when the complaint is based on specific, available materials like a video.

By examining both the complaint and the underlying materials (such as the video transcript), the court can accurately assess whether the essential ingredients of the alleged offence are actually present.

The Court held that if it were restricted to only the complaint, even a baseless accusation lacking the required legal ingredients could wrongly trigger the strict bar on anticipatory bail under Section 18.
Therefore, in cases where the evidence is documentary or digital and readily available, courts should have the discretion to look at that material to conduct a meaningful prima facie review.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that courts should have the discretion to look into the materials upon which a complaint has been registered, in addition to the complaint itself. If a prima facie reading of both the complaint and these materials reveals that the necessary ingredients of an offence under the Act are not made out, then the bar on anticipatory bail under Section 18 does not apply, and the court can consider the bail plea on its merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Court can, in exceptional cases, exercise power under Section 482 CrPC for quashing cases to prevent misuse of the Act's provisions.

law.name: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)
law.description: Grants High Courts inherent power to make orders necessary to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

law.name: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
law.description: Grants High Courts extraordinary jurisdiction to issue certain writs.

application.description: The Supreme Court affirmed that the power to quash cases under Section 482 of the CrPC can be exercised in exceptional circumstances to prevent the misuse of the provisions of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.
The Court noted that this legal position is clear and well-settled, and no arguments were presented to challenge it.

It was clarified that this inherent power to quash proceedings lies with the High Court, which can also exercise its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution for the same purpose.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court can, in exceptional cases, exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash cases in order to prevent the misuse of the Act's provisions.

issue.issue_text: Whether bail can be granted to a person who has not been arrested and for whose arrest no warrants have been issued.

facts: The case involved petitioners who were at liberty, had not been arrested, and for whom no arrest warrants had been issued.
law: The court established that the very concept of bail presupposes some form of prior restraint or custody.

Under the Criminal Procedure Code (specifically Sections 496, 497, and 498), bail can only be granted to a person who has been arrested, detained without a warrant, or who appears or is brought before a court.
application: The court reasoned that since bail is a release from restraint, it cannot be granted to someone who is not under any restraint.
It determined that the petitioners did not fall into the categories of persons eligible for bail under the Code, as they were not in custody.
The court stated that for the question of bail to even be considered, a person must be liable to arrest and must surrender themselves to the court.
It explicitly held that no bail can be allowed for a person who is at liberty and for whom no arrest warrants have been issued.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that bail cannot be granted to a person who has not been arrested and for whom no arrest warrants have been issued, thus answering the question in the negative.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 18 of the Act, which bars the application of Section 438 of the Code, is not violative of Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution; however, the Court can, in exceptional cases, exercise its power under Section 482 of the Code to quash cases to prevent the misuse of the Act's provisions.
obiter: A penal statute must receive strict construction.
A principle of statutory interpretation embodies the policy of the law, which is in turn based on public policy.
The court presumes, unless the contrary intention appears, that the legislator intended to conform to this legal policy.

We recommend the acceptance of this suggestion. We are further of the view that this special power should be conferred only on the High Court and the Court of Session, and that the order should take effect at the time of arrest or thereafter.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the power to grant pre-arrest bail should not be used liberally so as to convert the jurisdiction into a standard Section 438 CrPC proceeding, the High Court can and must exercise its power in very exceptional cases. Specifically, where no prima facie offence is made out in the FIR, the court must intervene to prevent a miscarriage of justice or abuse of the legal process, as not doing so would defeat the very purpose of justice.
legal_tests_applied: A penal statute must receive strict construction.

When considering an application for pre-arrest bail in cases under the Act, the court must balance two interests: ensuring the power is not used so broadly as to replicate Section 438 of the Criminal Procedure Code, while also using it sparingly in exceptional cases where no prima facie offence is evident from the FIR to prevent a miscarriage of justice or abuse of process.
The power under Section 482 CrPC can be exercised in exceptional cases to quash proceedings to prevent the misuse of the Act's provisions on settled parameters.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the proposition that bail could be granted to a person who has not been arrested and for whom no arrest warrant has been issued, reasoning that any special power for pre-arrest bail should only take effect 'at the time of arrest or thereafter'.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the respondent's position on the specific issue of bail for a non-arrested person, concluding that any such protective order should only become effective 'at the time of arrest or thereafter', implying that the event of arrest is a necessary precursor to bail.
policy_considerations: The court must balance its powers to prevent the misuse of the Act by unscrupulous petitioners while ensuring that a failure to act in exceptional cases does not result in a miscarriage of justice or abuse of the process of law.
A liberal use of the power to grant pre-arrest bail would defeat the intention of Parliament in enacting the specific provisions of the Act.

The principle that a penal statute must be strictly construed is a principle of legal policy, based on public policy, which the court presumes the legislator intended to conform to unless a contrary intention is apparent.
